summary: Reviewed the dvpwa 'sqli' aiohttp application (DAO layer, views, routes, middlewares, auth utilities, Jinja2 setup, config and schema). This is an intentionally vulnerable training app and the review confirms that: an unauthenticated SQL injection in Student.create, application-wide stored/reflected XSS from a disabled Jinja2 autoescape, globally disabled CSRF protection, unsalted MD5 password hashing, a session cookie with HttpOnly disabled, and missing authorization on state-changing endpoints. Overall risk is critical: the SQL injection and stored XSS are remotely reachable without authentication. Coverage was the Python source and templates; static JS/CSS assets and binary font files were not reviewed.

findings.title: SQL injection in Student.create via string formatting of student name
findings.description: Student.create builds the INSERT statement by interpolating the user-supplied name directly into the SQL string with Python % formatting instead of using a bound parameter. It is reachable without authentication: the students view handles POST /students/ and calls Student.create(conn, data['name']) with the raw form field (sqli/views.py:54-57). An attacker can submit a crafted name such as x'); DROP TABLE students;-- or a value with embedded single quotes to break out of the string literal and inject arbitrary SQL, enabling data exfiltration, modification, or destruction. Because CSRF is also disabled and the endpoint is unauthenticated, this is trivially exploitable.
findings.evidence:
q = ("INSERT INTO students (name) "
     "VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name})
...
await cur.execute(q)

Source: views.py students() -> await Student.create(conn, data['name']) with data = await request.post().
findings.recommendation: Use a parameterized query and let the driver quote the value: await cur.execute("INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (%(name)s)", {'name': name}). Never build SQL with % / f-strings / concatenation from user input.

findings.title: Application-wide XSS: Jinja2 autoescape disabled globally
findings.description: aiohttp_jinja2 is configured with autoescape=False, so every template expression renders user data as raw HTML unless an explicit |e filter is added, which most templates omit. User-controlled values are reflected without encoding, producing stored and reflected XSS. The clearest stored sink is sqli/templates/course.jinja2:22 which renders {{ review.review_text }} unescaped; review_text is attacker-controlled free text submitted (unauthenticated) via POST /courses/{id}/review (views.py:119-129, Review.create). Other unescaped sinks fed by user input include course.jinja2:14-15 ({{ course.title }}, {{ course.description }}) and students.jinja2:16 ({{ name }}). An attacker stores <script>...</script> in a review and it executes in every visitor's browser; combined with the non-HttpOnly session cookie this allows session hijacking.
findings.evidence:
setup_jinja(app, loader=PackageLoader('sqli', 'templates'),
            context_processors=[...],
            autoescape=False)

Sink: course.jinja2 line 22 -> {{ review.review_text }} (no |e). Source: views.review() -> Review.create(conn, course_id, review_text) with review_text = data.get('review_text').
findings.recommendation: Enable autoescaping (autoescape=True, or autoescape=select_autoescape(['html','jinja2'])) in setup_jinja, and only mark explicitly trusted values as safe. Do not rely on per-template |e filters.

findings.title: CSRF protection disabled by commenting out csrf_middleware
findings.description: The csrf_middleware (defined in sqli/middlewares.py:25-38, which validates the _csrf_token form field against the session) is commented out of the application middleware list, so no CSRF validation runs on any request. All state-changing POST endpoints (login at /, create student, create course, submit review, evaluate/assign marks) accept cross-site forged requests. Although the forms still embed a csrf_token, nothing checks it. An attacker can auto-submit forms from a malicious page to perform actions in a victim's authenticated context.
findings.evidence:
middlewares=[
    session_middleware,
    # csrf_middleware,
    error_middleware,
]

csrf_middleware exists and is functional in middlewares.py but is never registered.
findings.recommendation: Re-enable csrf_middleware in the middleware list so that every POST validates the per-session _csrf_token. Ensure it runs after session_middleware.

findings.title: Passwords hashed with unsalted MD5
findings.description: User.check_password compares the stored hash against md5(password). Passwords are therefore stored as unsalted MD5 digests (see migrations/fixtures), a fast, broken hash with no salt and no work factor. If the users table is read (e.g. via the SQL injection above or any DB disclosure), passwords are recoverable near-instantly via rainbow tables or brute force, and identical passwords yield identical hashes.
findings.evidence:
def check_password(self, password: str):
    return self.pwd_hash == md5(password.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest()
findings.recommendation: Use a memory-hard, salted password hash such as Argon2id, bcrypt, or scrypt (e.g. via passlib or argon2-cffi). Rehash existing passwords on next login and compare using the library's constant-time verify.

findings.title: Session cookie created with HttpOnly disabled
findings.description: RedisStorage is instantiated with httponly=False, so the session cookie is readable by client-side JavaScript. Combined with the application-wide XSS (autoescape disabled), an injected script can read document.cookie and exfiltrate the session identifier, leading to full account/session takeover. The Secure flag is also not set, so the cookie can be transmitted over plaintext HTTP.
findings.recommendation: Create the storage with httponly=True (the default) and set secure=True so the session cookie is inaccessible to JavaScript and only sent over HTTPS. Consider samesite='Lax' or 'Strict' as well.

findings.title: Missing authorization on state-changing endpoints (create/evaluate/review)
findings.description: The @authorize decorator (sqli/utils/auth.py) is applied only to logout. All other state-changing handlers have no authentication or authorization check, even though the UI only exposes their forms to logged-in or admin users. The evaluate handler assigns marks to students for a course with no auth check at all (views.py:134-153), so any anonymous user can POST /students/{id}/evaluate/{course_id} and set grades. The same gap applies to student creation (views.py:51-60), course creation (views.py:83-93), and review submission (views.py:111-131). Access control is enforced only in templates ({% if auth_user.is_admin %}), not on the server side.
findings.evidence:
async def evaluate(request: Request):
    ...
    await Mark.create(conn, student_id, course_id, data['points'])

No @authorize()/@authorize(ensure_admin=True) on evaluate, students, courses, or review; only logout uses it.
findings.recommendation: Enforce authorization server-side on every state-changing endpoint, e.g. decorate privileged handlers with @authorize(ensure_admin=True) (admin-only actions like evaluate) or @authorize() for authenticated-only actions, rather than relying on template conditionals.
